No; imaging helps exclude other lesions but diagnosis can be made clinically with screening tools when imaging is unavailable.
faq.q: Is a brain MRI mandatory for diagnosis?

faq.a: Lower CD4 (<200) correlates with higher HAND prevalence, but impairment can occur at any CD4 level.
faq.q: How does CD4 count relate to HAND risk?

exam: What bedside tests would you use to screen a HIV‑positive patient for HAND and why? — IHDS or MoCA; quick, validated, detect early impairment.
A patient on efavirenz presents with worsening cognition; what is your next step? — Consider switching to a regimen with better CNS tolerability, e.g., dolutegravir‑based.
How do you differentiate HAND from CNS TB in a resource‑limited setting? — Look for fever, focal deficits, CSF pleocytosis; TB often has systemic signs and responds to anti‑TB therapy.
Explain why a high CNS Penetration Effectiveness (CPE) score ART regimen is preferred in HAND. — Improves viral suppression within the brain, reducing neuroinflammation.
A patient with CD4 150 and new gait disturbance has a normal CT; what is your management? — Start empiric anti‑TB and cryptococcal therapy while arranging lumbar puncture if possible.
What are the key components of long‑term follow‑up for HAND? — Regular neurocognitive screening, maintain viral suppression, treat co‑morbidities, and provide rehabilitation.
Why should high‑dose efavirenz be avoided in patients with severe HAND? — It can exacerbate neuropsychiatric symptoms and worsen cognition.
Describe the three HAND stages and how functional status guides treatment intensity. — ANI (no functional loss), MND (mild loss, rehab), HAD (severe loss, aggressive ART and supportive care).
ai.title: HIV-Associated Neurocognitive Disorder
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is a spectrum of cognitive impairment caused by HIV infection of the CNS. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment and exclusion of other causes, with staging by severity.

b: Use International HIV Dementia Scale (IHDS) or MoCA adapted for low‑resource settings
Require at least 2‑domain impairment for mild disorder, >2‑domain with functional decline for dementia
sections.p: HAND includes asymptomatic neurocognitive impairment, mild neurocognitive disorder, and HIV-associated dementia. Diagnosis requires documented HIV infection, neurocognitive testing showing decline, and exclusion of alternative etiologies.

b: ANI: neuropsych testing abnormal, daily function preserved
MND: mild functional impact, may need rehab
HAD: marked functional loss, requires aggressive management
sections.p: The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) staging: Asymptomatic Neurocognitive Impairment (ANI), Mild Neurocognitive Disorder (MND), HIV-Associated Dementia (HAD). Staging guides treatment intensity and follow‑up.

b: HIV viral replication in brain macrophages/microglia
Tuberculous meningitis or CNS TB
Cryptococcal meningitis
Severe anemia, malnutrition, hepatitis B co‑infection
Neurotoxic herbal remedies
sections.p: Direct HIV neuroinvasion is primary, but co‑infection and metabolic disturbances are common in East Africa.

b: Early: forgetfulness, difficulty concentrating
Mid: slowed speech, poor multitasking
Late: apathy, motor signs, dependence in ADLs
sections.p: Patients develop progressive memory loss, slowed psychomotor speed, impaired attention, and executive dysfunction. Advanced disease shows personality change, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence.
Investigations aim to confirm HIV CNS involvement and rule out mimics; many tests are unavailable in low‑resource hospitals, so clinical judgment is essential.

t.a: CD4 count and plasma HIV viral load
t.b: Assess systemic disease activity; low CD4 (<200) and high VL increase HAND risk
Identify reversible metabolic causes (e.g., hyponatremia, renal failure)

t.a: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (if meningitis suspected)
t.b: Detect TB, cryptococcus, or other infections; if unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture
Rule out space‑occupying lesions, opportunistic infections; if not available, rely on exam and response to therapy

b: New focal deficits → possible CNS TB or stroke
Seizures → consider cryptococcal meningitis or toxoplasmosis
Fever + headache → meningitis
sections.p: Rapid decline, focal neurological signs, seizures, or fever indicate an acute opportunistic infection requiring urgent treatment.

b: Optimize ART: use regimens with high CNS Penetration Effectiveness (e.g., dolutegravir‑based) and ensure adherence
Treat TB meningitis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol; monitor for drug interactions with ART
Treat cryptococcal meningitis with amphotericin B + flucytosine (if available) followed by fluconazole
Provide cognitive rehab, physiotherapy, and psychosocial support
Avoid high‑dose efavirenz in patients with severe neurocognitive decline due to neuropsychiatric side effects
sections.p: Control HIV replication, treat co‑infections, and provide neurorehabilitation. Choose drugs with good CNS penetration and minimal neurotoxicity.

b: Repeat IHDS or MoCA at each clinic visit
Ensure CD4 >200 and VL <50 copies/mL
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus
sections.p: Regular neurocognitive screening every 6‑12 months, maintain viral suppression, and address modifiable risk factors such as anemia and malnutrition.

b: Depression → mood symptoms predominate, improves with antidepressants
Alzheimer disease → prominent episodic memory loss, less motor involvement
CNS TB/cryptococcosis → focal signs, fever, CSF abnormalities
sections.p: Conditions that mimic HAND include depression, normal aging, and other opportunistic CNS infections.

b: Normal CD4 >350 may still have HAND if CNS viral reservoirs persist
IHDS may be falsely normal in highly educated patients; adjust for education level
sections.p: Normal CD4 or viral load does not exclude HAND; neurocognitive decline can occur despite virologic control.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid cognitive decline, new focal neurological signs, seizures, fever, or worsening functional status
